Pontus
pon'tus
n. (the Roman province along the southern shore of the Black Sea; home of Aquila, and first-named in Peter's address to the scattered elect)
From Greek Pontos, sea — the region taking its name from the Euxine, the Black Sea, on whose southern coast it lay. The Latin name preserves the Greek word for the water itself.

Biblical Definition

Pontus lies on the far northern rim of the world the New Testament knows, and it appears three times, each time with weight out of proportion to the mention. Men of Pontus were in Jerusalem at Pentecost and heard the wonderful works of God in their own tongue — the list begins “Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites… in Pontus, and Asia” (Act 2:9). Second, it gave the church one of its most valuable couples: “a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla” (Act 18:2), expelled from Rome by Claudius, met by Paul in Corinth, tentmakers who housed him, worked beside him, followed him to Ephesus and there took Apollos aside and expounded the way of God more perfectly. Third and last, Peter heads his address with it: “to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1Pe 1:1). The trajectory is worth marking. A province at the edge of the map sends pilgrims to Pentecost, receives the word, exports a craftsman couple who become pillars of two churches, and within a generation holds congregations addressed by an apostle as “elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father” (1Pe 1:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Pontus; it is a province of Asia Minor on the southern coast of the Euxine or Black sea.

expand to see more

PONTUS, n. A country and Roman province of Asia Minor, lying along the Euxine sea.

The name is the Greek word for the sea, taken from the water on which it borders.

Men of Pontus were at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost.

Aquila, the fellow labourer of Paul, was a Jew born in Pontus.

Peter addresses his first epistle to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus and the neighbouring provinces.

Key Scripture

Act 2:9 — "Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites, and the dwellers in Mesopotamia, and in Judaea, and Cappadocia, in Pontus, and Asia,"

Act 18:2 — "And found a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome:) and came unto them."

1Pe 1:1 — "Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia,"

1Pe 1:2 — "Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ: Grace unto you, and peace, be multiplied."

Modern Corruption

Peter's opening words are softened so that election becomes God's response to foreseen faith, and Priscilla's teaching of Apollos is enlisted to overturn what Paul says about the eldership.

expand to see more

Peter calls the believers of Pontus “elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father”, and the standard softening makes foreknowledge mean advance information — God saw who would believe and chose accordingly. That reading empties the word. In Scripture God's foreknowing of persons is His setting of love upon them beforehand, not His prediction of their behaviour: “whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom 8:29), and the objects are people, not facts about people. Election that depends on foreseen faith is election that depends on the creature, and it cannot be squared with a sentence that grounds the choosing in the Father, the sanctifying in the Spirit, and the obedience in the sprinkled blood of the Son.

The second corruption uses a Pontic couple to unsettle the New Testament's order for the church. Priscilla and Aquila took Apollos and “expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly” (Act 18:26), and the episode is offered as proof that Paul's restriction of the teaching office to men is cultural. It proves nothing of the sort. This is a married couple, together, instructing one man privately in their own household — not a woman holding the office of elder in a congregation. The dictionary holds the plain apostolic rule (1Ti 2:12; 1Ti 3:1-7) alongside the plain apostolic esteem for Priscilla, whom Paul calls his helper in Christ Jesus and thanks by name. Both stand; neither cancels the other.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek Pontos (G4195), Pontus; prognosis (G4268), foreknowledge; eklektos (G1588), elect; skenopoios (G4635), tentmaker; diaspora (G1290), dispersion.

expand to see more

Greek Pontos (G4195) — Pontus; the province named from the sea it borders.

Greek prognosis (G4268) — foreknowledge; in Scripture God's prior setting of love, not bare prediction.

Greek eklektos (G1588) — chosen, elect; the standing of the saints in this province.

Greek skenopoios (G4635) — tentmaker; the trade Aquila of Pontus shared with Paul.

Greek parepidemos (G3927) — sojourner, stranger; Peter's name for the scattered believers.

Usage

"“A certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus” — an exile who became a pillar."

"“Strangers scattered throughout Pontus” — the edge of the map, full of the elect."

"“In Pontus, and Asia” — the far province present at Pentecost."
